findings.item: FINDING 7 -- EVAL_AFF_MIN domain=(0.0,1.0), 'at 0.0 every expert with any mass SERVES ... below 0.0 an expert with no mass serves, and "serving none" is the reading that becomes unreachable'
findings.detail: THE ENDPOINT PROSE IS OFF BY ONE ENDPOINT, AND THE SAME SENTENCE IS IN src/eval/levers.py:425-427. The predecessor's test is `_p >= AFF_MIN`, an INCLUSIVE comparison, and the normalisation is `_v / _v.sum().clamp_min(1e-9)`, which sends a zero-mass expert to _p = 0.0 rather than to nan. So at AFF_MIN = 0.0 an expert with NO mass ALREADY serves (0.0 >= 0.0), 'serving none' is ALREADY unreachable at 0.0, and 0.0 is behaviourally identical to every negative value the pair refuses. The distinction the comment draws between 0.0 and below-0.0 does not exist in the operator it cites. Note the quoted fragment drops the `.clamp_min(1e-9)` -- and that clamp is precisely what makes the claim wrong. The DOMAIN is still defensible (it refuses values indistinguishable from an admitted endpoint, which costs nothing); the stated REASON for its low end is not, and this tree's rule is that no comment may claim past the mechanism. The honest half of the finding -- that src/eval/api.py::verdicts is a P6 stub that raises NotImplementedError and that the bound rests on the predecessor -- is true and I confirmed it.

unfinished.title: V3 -- src/eval/levers.py's aff_min endpoint sentence is wrong about its own operator, and the quoted fragment hides why
unfinished.reason: src/eval/levers.py IS one of the six owned files. The domain is fine; the sentence beside it is not, and this tree forbids a comment claiming past the mechanism.
unfinished.detail:
src/eval/levers.py:425-427 reads: 'at 0.0 every expert with any mass at all SERVES the domain ... below 0.0 an expert with no mass serves, and "serving none" is the reading that becomes unreachable.'
The cited operator is `_p >= AFF_MIN` and the cited normalisation is `_v / _v.sum().clamp_min(1e-9)` (self_organize.py:8964-8965). Two consequences the sentence gets backwards:
  (a) the comparison is INCLUSIVE, so at AFF_MIN = 0.0 an expert with zero mass ALREADY serves -- 'serving none' is unreachable AT 0.0, not only below it;
  (b) therefore 0.0 and EVERY negative value produce identical verdicts, so the low end of the pair refuses only values that are behaviourally indistinguishable from the endpoint it admits. That is harmless as a rule and empty as an argument.
The comment quotes the predecessor as `_p = _v / _v.sum()`, dropping `.clamp_min(1e-9)`. Without the clamp a zero-mass vector gives nan and `nan >= 0.0` is False, which is the ONLY reading under which the sentence would be true -- so the elision is exactly what makes the claim survive.
MEASURED, _v = [3.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0]: AFF_MIN = -0.5, -0.001, -0.0 and 0.0 all give serves=[T,T,T,T], serving-none=0; AFF_MIN=0.1 gives serves=[T,T,F,F], serving-none=2.
SHAPE OF THE EDIT: quote the clamp, and say that 0.0 is the value at which the threshold stops being one from below (every expert serves, zero-mass included) just as 1.0 is the value at which it stops being one from above. The pair itself need not move.
